prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A hundred and one butter lamps are offered to my uncle who is no more. Distraction proves fatal in death. A curtain of butter imprints in air. After the burning of bones, ashes are sent on pilgrimage. You are dead, go into life, we pray. My uncle was a man given to giggles in solemn moments. Memory springs like crocuses in bloom. Self conscious and precise. Without blurring the cornea, details are resuscitated. Dried yak meat between teeth. Semblance of what is. Do not be distracted, Uncle who is no more. He does not see his reflection in the river. The arching of speech over “s” as he is becoming. Curvature of spine as it cracked on a misty morning. A shadow evades the wall. You are no more, Uncle who is no more. Every seven days he must relive his moment of expiration. The living pray frequently amid burning juniper. Communication efforts require the right initiative. Somewhere along the line matters of motion and rest are resolved. Crows pick the last offerings. You are someone else, uncle no more.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Distraction, After, You

outputs.L1:
One hundred and one butter lamps are offered to my uncle, who is no more. Distraction proves fatal in death. A curtain of butter leaves its imprint upon the air. After the burning of bones, the ashes are sent on pilgrimage. You are dead; go into life, we pray.

My uncle was a man given to giggles in solemn moments. Memory springs forth like crocuses in bloom: self-conscious and precise. Without blurring the cornea, details are resuscitated—dried yak meat between teeth; the semblance of what is.

Do not be distracted, Uncle who is no more. He does not see his reflection in the river. The arching of speech over “s” as he is becoming. The curvature of his spine as it cracked on a misty morning. A shadow evades the wall.

You are no more, Uncle who is no more. Every seven days, he must relive his moment of expiration. The living pray frequently amid burning juniper. Communication efforts require the right initiative. Somewhere along the line, matters of motion and rest are resolved. Crows pick at the last offerings.

You are someone else, uncle no more.
outputs.L2:
One hundred and one lamps of butter are presented in offering for my departed uncle. In the realm of death, even a lapse of attention can be deadly. Butter forms a veil, leaving its trace upon the air. When the bones have burned, the ashes are dispatched on a sacred journey. We pray: you have died; enter into life.

My uncle was the sort of man who would break into giggles during grave occasions. Remembrance rises suddenly, like crocuses opening in flower. He was exacting, careful, aware of himself. The particulars return without clouding the eye: dried yak meat caught between his teeth, the likeness of what remains. Do not lose focus, my uncle who is gone.

He no longer finds his face reflected in the river. His speech bends over the sound of “s” as he comes into being again. His spine curved as it snapped on a fog-soaked morning. A shadow slips away from the wall. You are gone now, uncle who is gone.

Every seventh day, he must pass once more through the instant of his dying. The living continue their prayers, often surrounded by the smoke of burning juniper. Attempts to communicate demand the proper effort. At some point, the questions of movement and stillness are settled. Crows peck at the final offerings. You have become another being, no longer my uncle.
outputs.L3:
A hundred and one butter lamps are offered in ritual remembrance of the speaker’s deceased uncle, their flames gathering like small, steady prayers against the darkness of loss. The act is both devotional and intimate: each lamp becomes an offering of light, a gesture meant to guide the dead and comfort the living. Around this ritual, the family and community pray for the uncle’s passage into the life after death, urging him onward while warning him not to be distracted by attachments, memories, or the familiar world he has left behind.

As the rites unfold, vivid memories of the uncle return with striking clarity. The speaker recalls not only his character and presence but also the small physical details that made him unmistakably himself. These recollections bring him briefly back into the room, alive in the mind even as the rituals acknowledge his death. The poem’s emotional force comes from this tension between absence and presence: the uncle is gone, yet he remains intensely visible through memory.

The poem blends funeral rites with sensory images of offerings, ashes, and burning juniper. These elements create an atmosphere of solemn transition, where smoke, flame, and prayer mark the boundary between one state of being and another. Death is not presented simply as an ending, but as a passage requiring attention, guidance, and release. The living do what they can through ritual, while also confronting the mystery of what lies beyond.

By the end, the uncle is imagined as undergoing a transformation. He is no longer only the man remembered by his family, with his familiar traits and earthly identity. Instead, he is becoming someone else, moving beyond the limits of his former life. The poem therefore becomes both an elegy and a meditation on change: it honors the uncle as he was, while imagining his journey into an unknown existence beyond death.
outputs.L4:
Butter lamps flicker in the dim room, their small flames wavering as if they are breathing with the gathered mourners. Around them, the air is thick with the scent of smoke, incense, and warm clarified butter. Ashes rest nearby, fragile and pale, reminding everyone that the body has become something light enough to scatter, something that can no longer be held in the old familiar way. Prayers rise and fall in a steady rhythm, spoken softly and then repeated, as though each word is a step laid down for the dead to follow. Offerings are placed with care: food, flowers, grains, water, and gestures of devotion meant to nourish the journey beyond this life.

At the center of these rituals is the memory of an uncle who has died. He is not remembered only as a body prepared for departure, but as a person made vivid through small and intimate details. His voice, his habits, the way he moved through a room, the things he loved, and the stories he carried all return in fragments. These memories keep him close even as the rituals acknowledge that he must go on. The living gather around what remains, but they also gather around what cannot be burned or buried: affection, gratitude, grief, and the lingering shape of a life shared with others.

The text presents mourning not simply as sadness, but as a passage marked by ritual action. Lighting lamps, tending ashes, reciting prayers, and making offerings all become ways of participating in the mystery of death. These acts give form to grief, allowing sorrow to move through the hands, the voice, and the body. They also suggest that death is not only an ending, but a transition. Through ritual, the dead are guided toward transformation, toward another state of being that the living may not fully understand but can still honor.

Memory works alongside ritual. While prayers help direct the uncle’s spirit onward, remembrance keeps his presence alive among those who remain. The details of his life become offerings of another kind. To recall him is to refuse the emptiness that death can bring. It is to say that a person’s meaning does not vanish when the body is gone. In this way, mourning becomes both release and preservation: the dead are allowed to depart, yet they remain woven into the lives of those who loved them.

The imagery of flames, ashes, prayers, and offerings creates an elegiac atmosphere, full of tenderness and reverence. The butter lamps burn briefly, like human lives, but their light also suggests continuity and hope. Ashes speak of impermanence, yet they also mark transformation. Prayers acknowledge helplessness before death, but they offer a path through that helplessness. Together, these images show how ritual helps the living face loss without surrendering to despair.

Ultimately, the text suggests that mourning is a sacred negotiation between absence and presence. The uncle is gone, yet he is still felt. His body has changed, yet his memory continues to illuminate the minds of those who survive him. Ritual gives the living something to do when grief feels unbearable, and memory gives them something to hold when the person himself can no longer be touched. Through these acts, death becomes not merely a rupture, but a passage shaped by love, meaning, and connection.
outputs.L5:
**Distraction, After, You**

After you, everything became a distraction.

The ticking clock sounded louder than before. The phone lit up, but every message felt empty. Songs played in the background, yet each melody somehow led back to the memory of your voice. Even ordinary places changed—the café on the corner, the quiet street at dusk, the chair by the window. They all seemed to wait for someone who was no longer there.

I tried to stay busy. I filled my days with work, conversations, errands, and plans. I told myself that movement would make forgetting easier. But distraction is a strange thing; it keeps the hands occupied while the heart remains still. No matter how far I walked or how much noise surrounded me, there was always a quiet space inside me shaped exactly like you.

After you, I learned that missing someone is not always dramatic. Sometimes it is gentle. It appears in small moments: reaching for my phone to tell you something funny, hearing your favorite song, or waking from a dream where nothing had changed.

And still, life continues. The days pass. The world keeps turning. Slowly, the distractions become less like hiding and more like healing. After you, I am learning how to be myself again—not the same as before, but stronger, softer, and more aware of what love can leave behind.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about Tibetan Buddhist death rituals for a deceased uncle, using imagery of butter lamps, juniper smoke, ashes, crows, memory, and reincarnation.
counterfactuals.output:
For my uncle, the butter lamps are lit one by one, small suns trembling in their brass cups, each flame leaning toward the next as if listening. Juniper smoke climbs the morning air in blue threads, carrying our prayers over the roof, over the valley, toward the high passes where snow keeps its own silence. We whisper your name, then let it go, because even a name is only a coat worn for one life.

The monks’ voices rise and fall like wind moving through prayer flags. In the bowl, the ashes are pale as moon dust, and I think of your hands—warm, broad, smelling of tea and wool, turning beads through years of weather. Outside, crows gather on the wall, black syllables against the sky, watching with bright eyes as if they know the road between worlds. One lifts its wings and becomes a question.

Memory is the last meal we offer you: the stories, the laughter, the old griefs softened by smoke. We feed the flames with butter; we feed the air with juniper; we feed the unseen path with mantras, hoping they make a bridge of sound beneath your feet. If the self is a lamp, then death is not the darkness, but the hand that moves the flame to another room.

Go gently, Uncle. May the fearful visions dissolve like mist over the river. May every crow be a messenger, every ash a seed, every prayer a door opening. Somewhere, a child will draw a first breath, and the world will begin again—unaware, radiant, carrying a spark we once knew as you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an elegiac experimental poem in fragments, addressed to “Uncle who is no more,” blending grief, ritual offerings, and surreal details of the body after death.
counterfactuals.output:
**Uncle who is no more,**

I bring rice in a brass bowl.  
I bring sesame, black as last words.  
I bring water cupped in my hands—  
it keeps leaking through the lines of my life.

Your name  
is a small lamp  
trying not to go out.

*

At dawn they said: body.  
Not you.  
Body.

The mouth packed with silence.  
The toes tied together like two frightened birds.  
Cotton blooming in the nostrils—  
white flowers for a country without air.

Someone closed your eyes  
and the room became older than history.

*

Uncle who is no more,

I wanted to ask if death is heavy,  
if the spine becomes a rope bridge,  
if the heart, finished with its red labor,  
folds itself like a tired flag.

But the priests were reciting.  
The smoke was climbing.  
The ghee hissed in the flame  
like a secret returning to its snake.

*

We circled you.

Around the pyre, around the fact,  
around the hole your absence made  
in the family photograph.

A crow landed on the wall  
and tilted its head—  
black witness, small judge,  
messenger with a beak full of dusk.

We waited for it to eat.

We waited for you to accept.

*

Your hands—

how strange that hands can become  
objects among objects.

Hands that broke mangoes open.  
Hands that blessed my head.  
Hands that counted coins, pills, rosary beads.  
Hands now emptied of weather.

I touched your knuckles.  
They were cool temples  
where no god answered.

*

Uncle who is no more,

tonight I place milk beside your shadow.  
I place fruit cut into moons.  
I place incense at the door  
so you may find the house by smell.

Come if you can.

Come as ash on the threshold.  
Come as a moth striking the bulb.  
Come as the cough in an empty room.  
Come as the dream in which you are younger  
and do not yet know us.

*

The body after death  
becomes a grammar we cannot read.

The jaw slack: unfinished vowel.  
The chest still: erased drum.  
The skin yellowing toward wax, toward turmeric,  
toward the color of old wedding silk.

Under the tongue, perhaps,  
one last syllable curled like a seed.

*

We fed the fire your name.

It ate slowly.

Bone cracked—  
a dry branch in the mind.

Smoke entered the sky  
with your shoulders, your eyebrows,  
the scar on your knee,  
the exact weight of your laughter.

Who will return these things?

*

Uncle who is no more,

I am told the soul travels south.  
I am told there is a river.  
I am told the dead are hungry.

So I make balls of rice,  
round as planets,  
soft as apologies.

I set them down  
for the part of you  
that still remembers having a mouth.

*

In the courtyard, the dogs howled  
at nothing we could see.

The mirror was covered.  
The clock continued its cruel profession.  
A child asked where you had gone  
and everyone became busy with plates.

Above us, the fan turned and turned—  
a slow helicopter  
unable to rescue anyone.

*

What is mourning  
but housekeeping for the invisible?

We sweep.  
We bathe.  
We wash the cloth.  
We tie the thread.  
We whisper instructions  
to one who has already crossed the room  
without opening the door.

*

Uncle who is no more,

forgive the living.

We are awkward with departure.  
We mistake ashes for endings.  
We keep your slippers  
as if feet might bloom back into them.

In the cupboard, your shirt  
still holds the shape of your absence.

I press my face to it.

Dust. Camphor. Sunlight.  
A faint medicinal sweetness.

Almost you.  
Not you.

*

At night my grief grows antlers.

It grazes beside my bed.  
It knocks its soft skull  
against the window.

I let it in.

Together we listen  
to the house digest your death.

*

Tomorrow I will offer water again.

I will pour it eastward,  
westward,  
into the root of the tulsi,  
into the throat of the earth.

Take this, Uncle.

Take this shining thread.  
Take this river made of hands.  
Take this meal of breath and remembering.

If you are ash, be ash blessed by rain.  
If you are smoke, be smoke that finds stars.  
If you are nothing,  
let nothing be gentle.

*

Uncle who is no more,

your absence sits with us  
cross-legged,  
eating from every plate.

We do not ask it to leave.

We light the lamp.  
We lower our voices.  
We learn the ritual of carrying you:

not in the arms—  
they failed;

not in the fire—  
it finished;

but in the mouth,  
where your name  
dissolves and returns,

dissolves and returns,

like water  
offered  
to the dead.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical meditation on the 49-day bardo after an uncle’s death, with repeated prayers, butter lamps, yak meat, rivers, shadows, and the line “You are dead, go into life.”
counterfactuals.output:
For forty-nine days  
we kept the house speaking softly,  
as if your name were a bird  
resting on the sill.

Each dawn, another butter lamp—  
small sun in a brass bowl—  
its trembling gold  
leaning toward the next world.

We prayed until the words  
lost their edges:

May you not be afraid.  
May you know the path.  
May you recognize the light.  
May you be free.

Uncle, the kettle steamed.  
The floorboards remembered your weight.  
Your coat hung by the door  
like a patient shadow  
waiting to be filled.

We set out yak meat,  
salted and dark,  
for the living mouths,  
for the old customs,  
for the hunger that remains  
after the body is gone.

Outside, the river kept turning  
over its stones,  
over its cold syllables,  
as if it too had been instructed  
to carry what it could not keep.

For forty-nine days  
the prayers returned—  
beads through fingers,  
smoke through rafters,  
wind through the juniper:

May you not cling to the doorway.  
May you not follow the voices.  
May you not mistake the shadows  
for home.

At night, the mountains  
lowered their blue foreheads  
to the valley.  
Dogs barked at nothing,  
or at what only dogs can see.  
The lamps burned down  
to small pools of silence.

And still we whispered:

You are dead, go into life.  
You are dead, go into life.  
You are dead, go into life.

Not as command,  
but as mercy.  
Not as farewell,  
but as a hand opened  
after holding too long.

Uncle, if the bardo is a river,  
may you cross it.  
If it is a field of shadows,  
may you walk through.  
If it is a room of mirrors,  
may you know which face  
is only fear  
and which is light.

We ate. We wept. We washed bowls.  
We fed the lamps.  
We folded your blankets.  
We listened for signs  
in flame, in dream,  
in the river’s black tongue.

Forty-nine days—  
a bridge made of breath,  
a road made of prayer,  
a door made of fire.

May you not be afraid.  
May you know the path.  
May you recognize the light.  
May you be free.

And when the last lamp flickered,  
when the smoke thinned  
into morning,  
when the river carried  
the final ashes of night away,

we spoke your name once more  
and let it go ahead of us:

You are dead, go into life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate a contemporary prose-poetry style: mourn a dead uncle through precise sensory images, Buddhist funeral rites, repetition, and philosophical reflections on motion, rest, and becoming.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the monks arrive in saffron the color of marigold pollen, the color of the last light on a persimmon before it softens into itself. They step out of their sandals and the floor accepts them without sound. Incense begins its thin animal motion through the room, nosing the rafters, entering our hair, our cuffs, the salt at the corners of our mouths.

My uncle lies still.

Still, but not absent.

Still, but the body is not the measure of departure.

We have washed him with warm water and cotton cloth. We have combed his hair in the direction it always wanted to go. Someone has placed white flowers near his hands, and his hands, which once split kindling, lifted bowls of rice, repaired a radio with a butter knife, now hold nothing. Or perhaps they hold the entire room in their refusal to grasp.

The bell is struck.

Its sound widens, then thins, then becomes a thread pulled through the ear into the chest. The monks chant the sutras, syllables rising and falling like breath sleeping inside another breath. I do not understand every word, but I understand the going-on of sound, the way it keeps moving after the mouth closes. I understand that grief is also a chant: it repeats because it cannot arrive.

Uncle, you were always in motion.

Your bicycle leaning blue against the guava tree. Your cigarette smoke traveling upward while you looked downward at the soil. Your laugh leaving before you did, entering the next room ahead of your body. Your knife tapping garlic into fragments. Your old truck coughing itself awake. Your shadow crossing the courtyard at noon, carrying a bucket, carrying rainwater, carrying the day from one task to another.

Now we sit around you and practice stillness badly.

My aunt folds and unfolds a handkerchief until it becomes a small white bird that will not fly. My cousin stares at the tea cooling in its cup, the leaves gathering at the bottom like thoughts after speech. Outside, a dog barks at the gate, then forgets why. A fly moves over the window screen with its tiny dark hands. Even the dust is traveling through the gold bar of sunlight. Even the wax softens and descends.

Nothing rests. Not even the dead.

The body rests, yes, under flowers, under cloth, under the gaze of everyone who cannot stop looking. But the body is also changing: cooling, paling, returning its borrowed heat to the morning. The breath has gone somewhere we cannot follow with our lungs. The name remains and moves from mouth to mouth. Uncle. Uncle. Uncle. Each time we say it, you become both nearer and less containable.

The monk speaks of impermanence.

How everything compounded comes apart. How every arrival is already a leaving dressed in ordinary clothes. How the river is not one river, though we point and call it by one name. How the flame passes from candle to candle without being the same flame, without being entirely different.

I watch the incense ash lengthen, bend, and fall.

This is instruction.

I watch my mother press her palms together, knuckles trembling.

This is instruction.

I watch your face become peaceful because we need it to be peaceful.

This, too, is instruction.

When they carry you out, the hallway seems too narrow for so much ending. Shoes scrape. Someone sobs once, sharply, as if struck from within. The chanting continues, and the bell continues, and the air opens to receive the smoke from the burning paper offerings: houses, shirts, money, a little paper car bright as a toy. We send you what cannot be sent. We burn what cannot burn. We give form to our helplessness, then turn it to ash.

Ash lifts.

Ash settles.

Ash becomes the gray breath on our sleeves.

I think of becoming not as a path forward but as the trembling of every edge. Rice becoming steam. Steam becoming cloud. Cloud becoming rain on the roof where you once stood, fixing a leak with tar and a curse. Boy becoming man. Man becoming memory. Memory becoming story. Story becoming silence. Silence becoming the bell before it is struck.

Uncle, you are not moving, and yet you are everywhere in motion.

In the tea my aunt pours though no one drinks.

In the orange peel curling on the plate.

In the sandalwood smoke entering and leaving the room.

In the prayer beads clicking through the monk’s fingers, one small world after another.

In my own breath, which continues without asking permission, which betrays me by staying.

Later, after the cremation, we will gather the bones with chopsticks, two by two, careful as if lifting sleeping birds. We will see what the fire has written in white. We will place you in the urn, not because you fit there, but because grief needs a shape to carry.

For now the bell sounds again.

For now the incense leans.

For now your face is a moon reflected in water no hand can hold.

Uncle, be free of pain.

Uncle, be free of fear.

Uncle, if there is a shore, may you reach it.

If there is no shore, may you become the crossing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting, non-rhyming elegy from the perspective of someone performing death prayers for their uncle, mixing tender memory, ritual language, and strange visual metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
I wash my hands before I speak for him.

The water is cold,  
as if it has been waiting all night  
inside a stone animal.

Uncle,  
your name rests on my tongue  
like a small lamp covered in ash.

I stand where the mourners have thinned,  
where the carpet keeps the shape of knees,  
where the air is full of breath  
that has forgotten its owners.

O Most Merciful,  
receive him.  
O Keeper of the hidden door,  
make wide the narrowness.  
Let the questioning be gentle.  
Let the earth remember  
he was kind to children,  
that he carried oranges in his coat,  
that he laughed with his head thrown back  
as if the ceiling had opened.

I raise my hands.

They do not feel like mine.  
They are two pale birds  
released in a room without windows.

Behind my closed eyes  
I see him in the old kitchen,  
cutting bread with a pocketknife,  
salt on the table,  
the radio murmuring weather  
to the dead and the living alike.

He would call me by the wrong name  
and then the right one,  
as though love were a hallway  
with many doors.

Now I recite what must be recited.  
I place each word carefully  
on the black river between us.

Forgive him his sleep.  
Forgive him his anger.  
Forgive the years he folded  
and hid in his chest  
like letters written underwater.

The candles tremble.  
Their flames look like yellow insects  
feeding on silence.

Someone behind me weeps  
with the sound of a chair being dragged  
across an empty house.

Uncle,  
your shoes are still by the entrance.  
They point toward the world  
with terrible patience.

I ask for light in the grave,  
light in the ribs of the soil,  
light like milk poured through a crack  
in the sky.

I ask that he not be alone  
when the dark leans down  
to learn his face.

And if the angels come  
with their books of iron,  
let them find his good deeds  
glowing there—  
small, stubborn coals  
under the snow of his mistakes.

I finish the prayer.

No thunder answers.  
No veil lifts.

Only the room,  
breathing around his absence,  
and my own hands descending  
slowly,

as if lowering a bowl  
filled with stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
